emt-cardio-l01.q: An adult has a heart rate of 50 and a stroke volume of 60 mL. What is the cardiac output?
choices: 3.0 L/min
5.0 L/min
6.0 L/min
0.3 L/min
emt-cardio-l01.why: Cardiac output = rate x stroke volume: 50 x 60 mL = 3,000 mL, which is 3.0 L/min. Normal is about 5 L/min, so this patient is moving roughly 60 percent of normal output and will show signs of poor perfusion.

emt-cardio-l01.q: Why does a sustained heart rate of 200 starve the heart muscle itself?
choices: Fast rates raise afterload beyond what the ventricle can overcome
Coronary arteries fill during diastole, and a fast rate removes the filling time
The coronary arteries branch off the pulmonary artery at high rates
Contractility is fixed and cannot rise with rate
emt-cardio-l01.why: Coronary filling happens during relaxation, because contraction pinches those vessels shut. A very fast rate shortens diastole, cutting both ventricular filling and the heart's own blood supply. Coronaries always branch off the aorta, never the pulmonary artery.

emt-cardio-l02.q: A patient's monitor shows a ventricular escape rhythm at 32. What does that rate tell you about the conduction system?
choices: The SA node is firing normally but the atria are not contracting
Both the SA node and the AV junction have failed, and the ventricles are the last backup
The AV node is delaying the impulse too long
The Purkinje fibers are blocked
emt-cardio-l02.why: Intrinsic rates are SA 60-100, AV junction 40-60, ventricles 20-40. A rate in the thirties means the two faster pacemakers above have quit and the ventricle itself is keeping the patient alive.

emt-cardio-l02.q: Why does a defibrillator do nothing for asystole?
choices: Asystole requires a higher energy setting than an AED delivers
A shock stops electrical activity so the SA node can resume, and in asystole there is nothing to stop
Asystole is always caused by a mechanical problem the shock cannot reach
The AED cannot detect asystole
emt-cardio-l02.why: Defibrillation depolarizes everything at once to end chaos. Asystole is already electrically silent, so there is no chaos to reset. Compressions and finding a correctable cause are the treatment.

emt-cardio-l03.q: A patient reports chest pressure that comes on after climbing two flights of stairs, lasts about 4 minutes, and resolves completely with rest. This most likely represents:
choices: Stable angina
Unstable angina
Acute myocardial infarction
Pericarditis
emt-cardio-l03.why: Predictable exertional pain lasting 3-5 minutes and relieved by rest is stable angina, and no muscle dies. Unstable angina occurs at rest or is worse than the patient's usual pattern. Pericarditis pain changes with position and breathing.

emt-cardio-l03.q: Which of these findings makes a heart attack LESS likely but does not rule it out?
choices: Diaphoresis out of proportion to the setting
Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall
Pain radiating to the jaw
Nausea with shortness of breath
emt-cardio-l03.why: Reproducible chest wall tenderness points toward a musculoskeletal cause, but a meaningful number of infarct patients still have it, so it never rules one out. Diaphoresis, jaw radiation and nausea all raise suspicion rather than lower it.

emt-cardio-l04.q: Within how many minutes of patient contact should a 12-lead ECG be obtained on a suspected infarct, and why does that number matter?
choices: 30 minutes, because that is when muscle begins to die
10 minutes, because the tracing decides whether the hospital activates the cath lab before you arrive
60 minutes, to match the door-to-balloon standard
5 minutes, because aspirin cannot be given until it is done
emt-cardio-l04.why: The 10-minute target exists so the receiving hospital can activate its catheterization team early. Muscle begins to die at about 20-30 minutes, which is the reason for the urgency but not the target itself. Aspirin does not wait for the tracing.

emt-cardio-l04.q: You gave one nitroglycerin dose. Baseline blood pressure was 138/84 and is now 104/62. The patient still has pain. You should:
choices: Give a second dose immediately because the systolic is above 100
Recognize that the systolic has fallen more than 30 mmHg from baseline and hold further doses per protocol
Give two doses at once to catch up
Lay the patient flat and give the second dose
emt-cardio-l04.why: A drop of more than 30 mmHg from baseline is a stop point even when the absolute number still looks acceptable. Doubling doses is never correct, and laying a chest pain patient flat does not make nitroglycerin safe.

emt-cardio-l05.q: Why does sitting an acute pulmonary edema patient upright with the legs dependent help immediately?
choices: It increases afterload, which strengthens contraction
Gravity pools blood in the legs and drops preload, so the failing ventricle has less to handle
It raises the blood pressure, which improves coronary flow
It allows the patient to cough more forcefully
emt-cardio-l05.why: Dependent legs hold blood away from the chest, reducing preload within seconds. Raising afterload would make a failing ventricle worse, and the blood pressure in acute pulmonary edema is usually already high.

emt-cardio-l05.q: A patient in acute pulmonary edema has a blood pressure of 196/108. This high reading is best explained by:
choices: An error in cuff size
Systemic vasoconstriction as the body clamps down, which is typical in this presentation
Cardiogenic shock developing
Right-sided heart failure
emt-cardio-l05.why: In acute decompensated left heart failure the sympathetic response constricts vessels, so the pressure is usually high, not low. A low pressure in this picture would suggest cardiogenic shock, which is a different and more dangerous problem.

emt-cardio-l06.q: Your resuscitation ran 10 minutes and your hands were on the chest for 5 of them. What was your compression fraction, and is it acceptable?
choices: 50 percent, which meets the standard
50 percent, which is below the 60 percent minimum
100 percent, because you compressed for the whole cycle
Compression fraction does not apply to BLS crews
emt-cardio-l06.why: Compression fraction is time compressing divided by total arrest time: 5 of 10 minutes is 50 percent, below the 60 percent floor. Falling short means arterial pressure collapses repeatedly and never rebuilds.

emt-cardio-l06.q: A pulseless adult is on a soft mattress. Before or while starting compressions you should:
choices: Compress harder to overcome the mattress
Move the patient to the floor or place a backboard beneath them
Raise the head of the bed to firm the surface
Begin ventilations first and delay compressions
emt-cardio-l06.why: A mattress absorbs your depth, so the chest never gets 2 to 2.4 inches of real compression. Pushing harder on a soft surface does not fix the geometry. Compressions still come first; a firm surface is arranged as part of starting them.

emt-cardio-l07.q: After the AED delivers a shock, how long do you perform CPR before the next rhythm analysis?
choices: 30 seconds
1 minute
2 minutes
Until the patient moves
emt-cardio-l07.why: The cycle is shock, immediate compressions, 2 minutes of CPR, then analyze again, switching compressors at the analysis. Checking sooner wastes the perfusion pressure you just rebuilt.

emt-cardio-l07.q: A pulseless patient has a very hairy chest and the pads will not stick. The correct action is:
choices: Delay defibrillation until you locate a razor
Press the pads down firmly, and if they still will not stick, pull them off to strip hair and apply a second set
Use anterior-posterior placement, which does not require adhesion
Abandon the AED and continue compressions only
emt-cardio-l07.why: Never delay defibrillation to shave. Press firmly first; if adhesion fails, ripping the first set off removes the hair and a second set sticks. Every placement requires skin contact, including anterior-posterior.

emt-cardio-l08.q: A family member says the patient has a DNR but cannot produce it. In New Jersey you should:
choices: Withhold resuscitation based on the family's statement
Begin resuscitation, because the documentation must actually be available
Begin resuscitation only if the patient is under 65
Wait for law enforcement before deciding
emt-cardio-l08.why: A verbal report that a DNR exists does not by itself authorize withholding care; the document must be present and applicable. Starting resuscitation is the default, and it can be stopped if valid documentation is produced. Waiting to decide is itself a decision not to resuscitate.

emt-cardio-l08.q: Which is NOT one of the accepted reasons to stop a resuscitation you have already begun?
choices: The patient revives
Care is transferred to a provider of equal or higher level
The scene becomes unsafe
The family asks you to stop because the patient is elderly
emt-cardio-l08.why: Once started you continue until revival, transfer of care, rescuer exhaustion, scene danger, or a physician or protocol order to terminate. A family request during an active resuscitation is not on that list and does not substitute for valid documentation or medical control.

emt-cardio-l09.q: A patient is hypotensive with FLAT neck veins after a motorcycle crash. This combination points toward:
choices: Cardiogenic shock
Cardiac tamponade
Blood loss
Tension pneumothorax
emt-cardio-l09.why: Flat neck veins with hypotension means the tank is empty, which is hemorrhage. Cardiogenic shock, tamponade and tension pneumothorax all cause blood to back up, producing distended neck veins with the hypotension.

emt-cardio-l09.q: Which set of findings best matches a massive pulmonary embolism?
choices: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, clear lungs, and hypoxia that barely improves with oxygen
Gradual dyspnea, crackles to the mid-fields, high blood pressure and pink frothy sputum
Muffled heart sounds with a pulse pressure of 86/72
Absent breath sounds on one side with a deviated trachea
emt-cardio-l09.why: A clot blocks pulmonary flow, so the lungs sound clear while the patient stays hypoxic despite oxygen. Crackles with frothy sputum is pulmonary edema, the narrow pulse pressure is tamponade, and unilateral absent sounds with tracheal deviation is tension pneumothorax.

emt-cardio-l10.q: A patient's blood pressure reads 210/118. Before acting on that number you should first:
choices: Give the patient their own antihypertensive medication
Confirm the cuff is the correct size for the arm and recheck both arms
Place the patient flat to reduce cerebral pressure
Transport with lights and siren
emt-cardio-l10.why: A cuff that is too small reads falsely high, so confirm the equipment before treating the number. EMTs do not administer antihypertensives or lower blood pressure. Flat positioning and a high-stimulation transport both work against you here.

emt-cardio-l10.q: Which syncope history is LEAST concerning for a dangerous cardiac cause?
choices: Fainted while sprinting during a soccer game
Fainted while sitting in a chair with no warning
Fainted after standing in a hot line, with nausea and tunnel vision first
Fainted with chest pain and palpitations
emt-cardio-l10.why: A prodrome of nausea, sweating and tunnel vision with an obvious trigger is the classic benign vasovagal pattern. Exertional syncope, syncope with no warning while seated, and syncope with chest pain or palpitations are all cardiac red flags.

emt-cardio-l11.q: Why is the V4 electrode placed before V3?
choices: V3 is defined as midway between V2 and V4
V4 has the strongest signal and calibrates the others
V3 must sit above V4 on the rib
The cable order requires it
emt-cardio-l11.why: V3 has no landmark of its own; it is defined by the midpoint between V2 and V4. Placing V3 by guess first pushes every lateral lead out of position and can create or erase apparent elevation.

emt-cardio-l11.q: A 12-lead on a woman shows 1.6 mm of ST elevation in V2 and V3. Does this meet the elevation threshold?
choices: No, women require 2 mm in V2 and V3
Yes, the threshold in V2 and V3 is 1.5 mm for women
No, any anterior elevation requires 3 mm
Yes, because 1 mm is the threshold in every lead
emt-cardio-l11.why: V2 and V3 have their own thresholds: 2 mm for men and 1.5 mm for women. Every other lead uses 1 mm. Applying the limb-lead threshold everywhere over-calls anterior STEMI.

emt-cardio-l12.q: A 34-year-old woman who delivered a baby three weeks ago has sudden crushing chest pain. Which infarct mechanism is disproportionately common in this group?
choices: Decades of atherosclerotic plaque
Spontaneous coronary artery dissection
Cocaine-induced coronary spasm
Silent infarct from diabetic neuropathy
emt-cardio-l12.why: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection strikes younger women, including around pregnancy, without the usual plaque disease. Classic plaque rupture is uncommon at 34, and neither stimulant spasm nor diabetic neuropathy fits the history given.

emt-cardio-l12.q: Which habit catches the most atypical infarcts?
choices: Obtaining a 12-lead only when the patient reports chest pain
Obtaining a 12-lead for unexplained dyspnea, syncope, weakness, epigastric pain or diaphoresis in any adult
Waiting for an abnormal vital sign before obtaining a 12-lead
Relying on the heart rate to decide
emt-cardio-l12.why: Broadening the trigger beyond chest pain is what finds the women, diabetics and elderly patients who are missed. Normal vitals are common in infarct, and a beta blocker removes the compensating tachycardia you might have been waiting for.

emt-cardio-l13.q: A patient's ICD fired once. He is now alert, comfortable, and has normal vital signs. He wants to refuse transport. The correct response is:
choices: Honor the refusal, since a single shock means the device worked
Explain that a shock means he had a life-threatening rhythm and strongly encourage transport with a 12-lead and pads applied
Apply a magnet and then honor the refusal
Transport only if the device fires again in front of you
emt-cardio-l13.why: A discharge proves the device detected a lethal rhythm, so this is a transport with a 12-lead and pads on, not a refusal. Magnet application is a protocol and medical direction decision and does nothing to make a refusal safe.

emt-cardio-l13.q: A magnet placed over a PACEMAKER, as distinct from an ICD, will:
choices: Turn the pacemaker off entirely
Force asynchronous pacing at a fixed rate, usually around 85-100
Suspend shock therapy only
Have no effect at all
emt-cardio-l13.why: Over a pacemaker a magnet forces fixed-rate asynchronous pacing, ignoring the patient's own beats. Suspending shocks is what a magnet does over an ICD. It never turns the device off.

emt-cardio-l14.q: You place your stethoscope on an LVAD patient's left chest and hear nothing. This means:
choices: The device is functioning normally, since continuous flow is silent
The pump has stopped, which is the emergency
The patient has a pneumothorax
The stethoscope is in the wrong place; LVADs are heard at the apex only
emt-cardio-l14.why: A working continuous-flow pump makes an audible mechanical hum. Silence means it has stopped, and that is the finding that drives everything next: troubleshoot the controller, batteries and driveline, then decide about compressions per protocol.

emt-cardio-l14.q: Which assessment finding is expected and NORMAL in a stable continuous-flow LVAD patient?
choices: A palpable radial pulse of 72
No palpable pulse and a pulse oximeter that will not read
A cuff blood pressure of 118/76 by auscultation
A monitor showing a flat line
emt-cardio-l14.why: Continuous flow produces no pulsation, so pulses and pulse oximetry commonly fail and a standard cuff reading is often unobtainable; a doppler MAP of about 70-90 mmHg is the usual measurement. The monitor still shows the patient's own underlying rhythm, not a flat line.

emt-cardio-l15.q: You are alone with a 3-year-old found collapsed and pulseless, with no witness to the event. You should:
choices: Leave immediately to call for help and get the AED
Perform about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to call
Perform abdominal thrusts first in case of a foreign body
Wait for a second rescuer before starting
emt-cardio-l15.why: Unwitnessed pediatric collapse is usually hypoxic, so 2 minutes of CPR before leaving addresses the cause. A witnessed sudden collapse in an older child looks more like adult sudden cardiac arrest, and that one gets the call and AED first.

emt-cardio-l15.q: A child pulled from a pool has water visibly coming from the mouth. You should:
choices: Perform abdominal thrusts to clear the water
Ignore the water, begin ventilations, and keep suction ready for vomiting
Roll the child prone and compress the back
Withhold ventilation until the airway is completely dry
emt-cardio-l15.why: There is no meaningful volume of water to remove from the lungs, and abdominal thrusts cause vomiting and aspiration. Ventilation comes first in drowning because hypoxia is the cause, and vomiting should be expected and suctioned.

emt-cardio-l16.q: At roughly what core temperature does shivering stop, and why does its absence matter?
choices: Below about 35 C, and it means the patient is warming
Below about 32 C, and it means the patient is getting worse rather than better
Below about 28 C, and it has no clinical significance
Shivering never stops regardless of temperature
emt-cardio-l16.why: Shivering ceases below roughly 32 C, so a patient who was shivering and now is not has deteriorated, not improved. It is one of the easiest deterioration signs to misread as reassurance.

emt-cardio-l16.q: Why is a hypothermic arrest patient moved horizontally and handled gently?
choices: To prevent fractures in brittle bones
Because a cold ventricle is electrically irritable and jostling can trigger ventricular fibrillation
To avoid dislodging frostbitten tissue
Because the spine is always assumed to be injured in cold exposure
emt-cardio-l16.why: Cold myocardium fibrillates easily, and rough handling, hard lifts or sitting the patient up have all been associated with triggering it. Fractures and frostbite are real concerns but are not the reason for the horizontal, gentle rule.

emt-cardio-l17.q: Which arrest would NOT have termination rules applied to it?
choices: An unwitnessed arrest in a 70-year-old with no shock delivered and no ROSC
An arrest following a drug overdose
An arrest witnessed by a bystander in a 60-year-old with no ROSC after full ALS
A witnessed arrest in an 80-year-old with a valid DNR produced mid-code
emt-cardio-l17.why: Overdose, hypothermia, drowning, late pregnancy and pediatric arrest are transported rather than terminated in the field. The other scenarios are governed by the usual BLS and ALS termination criteria or by valid documentation.

emt-cardio-l17.q: After a termination, the family asks whether their father suffered. The best approach is:
choices: Say you cannot discuss it
Answer simply and honestly, and avoid speculating about the cause
Reassure them he felt nothing, regardless of what happened
Redirect them to the hospital
emt-cardio-l17.why: Answer what is asked, plainly and honestly, including the hard questions. Inventing reassurance and refusing to engage are both failures; speculation about the cause is what you avoid, not the conversation itself.

emt-cardio-l18.q: Which post-ROSC blood pressure target is correct?
choices: Systolic at least 90 mmHg, MAP at least 65 mmHg
Systolic at least 140 mmHg, MAP at least 100 mmHg
Systolic at least 70 mmHg, MAP at least 50 mmHg
No target; blood pressure is not managed after ROSC
emt-cardio-l18.why: The targets are a systolic of at least 90 and a MAP of at least 65. Post-arrest hypotension independently predicts death and poor neurologic outcome, so measuring it often and saying the number out loud early is a real EMT contribution.

emt-cardio-l18.q: During which phase of a post-ROSC transport do re-arrests most often occur?
choices: While the patient is stationary on the stretcher
During movement, such as the carry or the transfer
Only after arrival at the hospital
Re-arrest timing is random and cannot be anticipated
emt-cardio-l18.why: More re-arrests happen during movement than at any other point, which is why the carry is planned in advance: who holds the airway, who watches the monitor, where the pads cable runs, and where you stop if the pressure drops.

quiz.q: A 55-year-old is bleeding heavily from a femur fracture. His heart rate is 132 and his blood pressure is 92/70. Which component of stroke volume has primarily fallen?
choices: Preload
Contractility
Afterload
Heart rate
quiz.why: Blood loss empties the tank, so the ventricle has less to fill with and preload falls. Contractility is intact in a healthy heart, afterload is actually rising as vessels clamp down, and heart rate is not a component of stroke volume at all.

quiz.q: Which vessels carry oxygen-poor blood away from the heart and oxygen-rich blood back to it, reversing the usual rule?
choices: The vena cavae and the aorta
The pulmonary arteries and the pulmonary veins
The coronary arteries and the coronary sinus
The carotid arteries and the jugular veins
quiz.why: The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs and the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood back, the only pair that breaks the pattern. The vena cavae and aorta follow the usual rule, and the carotids and jugulars are systemic vessels.

quiz.q: A patient with an inferior wall infarct develops a heart rate of 38. The anatomic explanation is that the right coronary artery usually supplies:
choices: The pulmonary valve
The left anterior descending territory
The SA and AV nodes
The lateral wall of the left ventricle
quiz.why: In most people the right coronary artery feeds the SA and AV nodes along with the inferior wall, so an inferior infarct commonly produces bradycardia and blocks. The lateral wall is circumflex territory, and the LAD supplies the front wall.

quiz.q: Which physiologic problem is the actual cause of pulseless electrical activity?
choices: Chaotic electrical activity in the ventricles
Complete absence of electrical activity
A conduction block in the bundle of His
A mechanical failure of the pump or the circulation, not an electrical one
quiz.why: In PEA the wiring is working and producing an organized rhythm, but the pump or the plumbing cannot produce output: blood loss, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive embolism, or muscle too damaged to contract. Chaos is ventricular fibrillation and absence is asystole.

quiz.q: Which structure is the only electrical connection between the atria and the ventricles?
choices: The bundle of His
The Purkinje fibers
The coronary sinus
The SA node
quiz.why: The bundle of His is the sole electrical bridge across the fibrous ring separating atria from ventricles. The SA node is the pacemaker above it, the Purkinje fibers distribute the signal within the ventricles, and the coronary sinus is a vein.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old has crushing chest pressure for 25 minutes that has not stopped with rest or two of his own nitroglycerin tablets. Previously his pain always stopped after climbing stairs. This change means:
choices: His stable angina is simply worse today and needs no different management
He has progressed to at least unstable angina and must be treated as an infarct
The nitroglycerin has expired and the pain is unrelated
Pericarditis has developed
quiz.why: Pain at rest, lasting longer, or no longer relieved by nitroglycerin is the definition of unstable angina, and you cannot distinguish it from an infarct in the field. Treating it as anything less than an infarct is the error the question tests.

quiz.q: Which single physical finding do experienced providers trust most as a marker of a serious cardiac event?
choices: A blood pressure above 160 systolic
A heart rate above 100
Diaphoresis out of proportion to the setting
Pain radiating to the left arm only
quiz.why: Skin that is wet without a reason is the most trusted single field sign, because it reflects the autonomic response to a real physiologic threat. Vital sign abnormalities are frequently absent in infarct, and radiation patterns vary widely.

quiz.q: A 60-year-old with chest pain is found walking around the apartment gathering belongings. You should:
choices: Have him carry only light items
Allow walking if his SpO2 is above 94%
Allow him to walk to the ambulance to save time
Stop him from walking or carrying anything and move him by stretcher
quiz.why: Any exertion raises myocardial oxygen demand in a heart that is already short of supply. Stopping the patient from walking, carrying or helping move himself is one of the cheapest interventions in the call. Oxygen saturation has nothing to do with the decision.

quiz.q: A chest pain patient's wife offers you her own nitroglycerin because the patient forgot his at home. His systolic is 142. You should:
choices: Decline, because the medication must be prescribed to this patient
Give half a dose as a compromise
Give it only after contacting the wife's physician
Give it, because the drug and dose are identical
quiz.why: One of the mandatory conditions is that the medication is prescribed to this patient and you have the actual bottle. A spouse's prescription fails that test regardless of how similar the tablet is. Halving a dose does not change the authorization problem.

quiz.q: A patient with chest pain took tadalafil 30 hours ago. His systolic is 150. Nitroglycerin is:
choices: Acceptable, because more than 24 hours have passed
Contraindicated, because tadalafil requires a 48-hour window
Acceptable at half the usual dose
Contraindicated only if the systolic falls below 120
quiz.why: Sildenafil and vardenafil use a 24-hour window, but tadalafil is long acting and requires 48 hours. Combining them causes profound refractory hypotension. The blood pressure at the moment of the question does not change the interaction.

quiz.q: A 76-year-old with heart failure says he now sleeps sitting up in a recliner because lying flat makes him breathless. This symptom is called:
choices: Hepatomegaly
Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Orthopnea
Pleurisy
quiz.why: Orthopnea is breathlessness when lying flat, which is why patients count pillows. Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is specifically waking suddenly gasping hours into sleep. Pleurisy is pain with breathing and hepatomegaly is liver enlargement from right-sided failure.

quiz.q: A hypotensive-looking 83-year-old in obvious pulmonary edema has a systolic of 84. Which intervention is contraindicated?
choices: Monitoring and rapid transport
Sitting the patient upright
Oxygen titrated to 94-99%
CPAP at 5-10 cmH2O
quiz.why: CPAP requires a systolic above 90 because positive pressure in the chest reduces venous return and can drop the pressure further. Upright positioning, titrated oxygen and rapid transport all remain appropriate.

quiz.q: Why is a fluid bolus wrong in acute pulmonary edema?
choices: The patient already has too much volume, and more fluid adds to lungs that are already flooding
It raises the heart rate dangerously
Fluids are outside EMT scope in all cases
It dilutes the patient's cardiac medications
quiz.why: The problem is a ventricle that cannot move the volume it already has, so adding volume worsens the flooding. The reflex to bolus for a number is the trap. Scope of practice is not the reason the intervention is wrong.

quiz.q: Which single compression quality error most directly prevents the heart from refilling between beats?
choices: Compressing at 130 per minute
Leaning on the chest and failing to allow full recoil
Compressing to 2.4 inches
Switching compressors every 2 minutes
quiz.why: Incomplete recoil keeps pressure in the chest, so blood cannot return to fill the heart, and a heart that does not fill has nothing to eject. A rate of 130 is too fast but the recoil error is the one that directly blocks filling; 2.4 inches and 2-minute switches are correct practice.

quiz.q: Two rescuers are resuscitating a 4-month-old. Which compression technique is preferred?
choices: Two hands with fingers interlaced
Two fingers just below the nipple line
Two thumbs encircling the chest with hands wrapping around
Heel of one hand on the lower sternum
quiz.why: With two rescuers the two-thumb encircling technique is preferred for infants because it produces better depth and better blood pressure. Two fingers is the one-rescuer method. One- and two-handed adult techniques are far too much force for an infant.

quiz.q: About how much does survival fall for each minute without CPR and defibrillation in an adult cardiac arrest?
choices: Survival does not fall until 10 minutes have passed
quiz.why: Roughly 7-10% per minute, which is why the first three links in the chain of survival decide the outcome and why bystander CPR roughly doubles or triples survival. There is no grace period before the decline begins.

quiz.q: An AED announces no shock advised on a pulseless, apneic patient. Your immediate action is:
choices: Resume compressions immediately and continue for 2 minutes
Remove the pads and reapply them in anterior-posterior position
Wait for the AED to reanalyze
Check a carotid pulse for up to 10 seconds, then reassess
quiz.why: No shock advised means the rhythm is not shockable, not that the patient is fine. Go straight back to compressions for a full 2-minute cycle. Repositioning pads and waiting for the machine both waste perfusion time.

quiz.q: A pulseless 35-year-old woman is 30 weeks pregnant and the AED advises a shock. You should:
choices: Withhold the shock because of the pregnancy
Deliver the shock normally, because saving the mother is what saves the fetus
Reduce the energy setting manually
Shock only after the patient is tilted fully onto her left side
quiz.why: Pregnancy does not change defibrillation. Saving the mother is the only path to saving the fetus, and an AED has no operator-adjustable energy setting. Delaying a shock to reposition costs survival.

quiz.q: A cardiac arrest occurs at a poolside and the patient is lying in a puddle with a wet chest. Before applying pads you should:
choices: Use anterior-posterior placement and skip drying
Apply the pads immediately, since water improves conduction
Drag the patient clear of standing water and towel the chest dry
Wait for the patient to air dry
quiz.why: Water on the skin and standing water under the patient both shunt energy away from the heart and create a hazard for rescuers. Moving clear and toweling the chest takes seconds. Changing pad position does not solve a wet chest.

quiz.q: You achieve ROSC and the patient remains unresponsive without adequate breathing. Which set of actions is correct?
choices: Ventilate at 10 per minute, oxygen at 100% throughout, actively warm the patient
Ventilate at 30 per minute to lower carbon dioxide and protect the brain
Ventilate at 20 per minute, oxygen at 100%, remove the pads, transport to the closest hospital
Ventilate at 10 per minute, titrate oxygen to 92-98%, leave the pads on, obtain a 12-lead
quiz.why: The post-ROSC bundle is 10 breaths per minute, oxygen titrated down off 100%, pads left on because re-arrest is common, and a 12-lead that may change the destination. Hyperventilation and sustained hyperoxia are the two most common errors, and active warming is specifically avoided.

quiz.q: Which finding constitutes an obvious sign of death that justifies not starting CPR?
choices: Dependent lividity with rigor mortis
An unwitnessed arrest with an unknown downtime
A very elderly patient with multiple chronic conditions
A cold, stiff-feeling patient found outdoors in winter
quiz.why: Rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition, decapitation and injuries incompatible with life are the obvious signs. A cold stiff patient in winter may be profoundly hypothermic and is resuscitated. Age, comorbidity and unknown downtime never justify withholding CPR.

quiz.q: Mechanical CPR devices are best described as:
choices: More effective than manual CPR in improving survival
Equivalent in effectiveness, valuable because they keep quality constant during transport, stairs and extrication
Only appropriate after 20 minutes of manual CPR
Contraindicated during transport
quiz.why: The evidence shows no survival advantage over good manual CPR. Their value is consistency where humans cannot deliver it, and the pause to apply one must stay under 10 seconds with compressions continuing during setup.

quiz.q: A patient with a blood pressure of 86/72 after blunt chest trauma has distended neck veins and heart sounds you can barely hear. The narrowing gap between the systolic and diastolic numbers is called:
choices: Widened mean arterial pressure
Pulsus paradoxus
A narrowing pulse pressure
Orthostatic change
quiz.why: Pulse pressure is the difference between systolic and diastolic, and a narrowing one with muffled sounds and distended neck veins is the classic tamponade triad. Pulsus paradoxus is a different phenomenon involving variation with respiration, and orthostatic change refers to positional readings.

quiz.q: Which risk factor most strongly raises suspicion for pulmonary embolism in a patient with sudden dyspnea and clear lungs?
choices: A family history of hypertension
Daily aspirin use
A 40-pack-year smoking history
A leg cast worn for six weeks after surgery
quiz.why: Immobilization from a cast after surgery is a direct clot risk, as are long travel, cancer, pregnancy, birth control pills and prior clots. Smoking and family hypertension are cardiovascular risks generally, and aspirin use is if anything protective against clot formation.

quiz.q: Cardiogenic shock following a large infarct carries a mortality of roughly:
quiz.why: Mortality remains around 40-50% even in patients who reach the hospital alive, which is why it is the leading cause of death in that group and why rapid transport to a catheterization-capable center matters so much.

quiz.q: A patient with a suspected aortic dissection asks for the aspirin you normally give for chest pain. You should:
choices: Give 324 mg chewed as usual
Withhold it and contact medical control, because aspirin is a bleeding risk in a tearing vessel
Give 81 mg instead
Give it only if the systolic is above 140
quiz.why: Antiplatelet therapy in a vessel that is actively splitting adds bleeding risk, and nitroglycerin in a hypotensive dissection is dangerous. Tearing pain to the back with unequal arm pressures changes the treatment, so contact medical control before giving anything.

quiz.q: What distinguishes hypertensive emergency from hypertensive urgency?
choices: Whether the patient takes antihypertensive medication
The systolic exceeding 200 rather than 180
Evidence of an organ actively being injured
The presence of a headache alone
quiz.why: The numbers are similar in both; the emergency is defined by signs of active organ injury such as severe headache, visual change, confusion, seizure, chest pain, crackles or focal neurologic deficit. Medication history and a specific systolic cutoff do not define it.

quiz.q: Every syncope patient should receive which assessment that is easy to forget?
choices: A temperature by rectal route
A pupil measurement in millimeters
A peak flow measurement
A blood glucose check
quiz.why: Hypoglycemia is a common and treatable mimic of syncope, so glucose is checked on every one, along with full vitals, an injury survey from the fall and a 12-lead. Peak flow, rectal temperature and pupil sizing are not routine parts of a syncope workup.

quiz.q: You are placing chest electrodes on a woman with large breasts. The correct technique is:
choices: Place the chest electrodes under the breast tissue at the correct spaces
Move V4 through V6 one space higher to clear the tissue
Use limb leads only
Place V4 through V6 on top of the breast tissue for consistency
quiz.why: Electrodes go under the breast tissue at the anatomically correct intercostal spaces. Placing them on top or shifting them up changes the recorded picture enough to create or hide an infarct, and a limb-lead-only tracing is not a 12-lead.

quiz.q: A tracing shows ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which wall and artery does this pattern suggest?
choices: Anterior and septal wall, left anterior descending
Lateral wall, circumflex artery
Posterior wall, no identifiable artery
Inferior wall, right coronary artery
quiz.why: I, aVL, V5 and V6 look at the lateral wall, usually supplied by the circumflex. II, III and aVF are inferior and right coronary; V1 through V4 are anterior and septal and belong to the left anterior descending.

quiz.q: Your tracing is full of wandering baseline and spikes. The most likely cause is:
choices: Incorrect lead selection on the machine
A true arrhythmia requiring immediate transport
A mechanical problem such as a loose electrode, damp skin, a talking patient or a moving vehicle
A defective monitor requiring replacement
quiz.why: Most bad tracings are mechanical: dry the skin, shave a patch, brace the arms, ask the patient to stop talking, and record with the vehicle stopped. Assuming artifact is a rhythm, or that the machine is broken, both delay a usable tracing.

quiz.q: An inferior STEMI pattern appears and the paramedic asks for a V4R tracing. The reason is to check for:
choices: Left bundle branch block
Atrial enlargement
A posterior wall infarct
A right ventricular infarct, which changes whether nitroglycerin can be given
quiz.why: Inferior infarcts frequently involve the right ventricle, which is entirely preload dependent, so nitroglycerin can cause profound hypotension. V4R is how that is identified. Bundle branch block and atrial findings are read from the standard tracing.

quiz.q: An 82-year-old is brought in for a new fall and sudden weakness with no chest complaint. Which action best reflects current practice?
choices: Obtain a 12-lead, because dyspnea, falls, confusion and weakness are common infarct presentations in the very old
Defer the 12-lead unless the heart rate is abnormal
Obtain a 12-lead only if a family member reports chest pain
Treat it as a fall and assess for injury only
quiz.why: By the eighties, shortness of breath is a more common infarct presentation than chest pain, along with confusion, falls, weakness and syncope. Waiting for an abnormal vital sign misses these patients, especially those on beta blockers.

quiz.q: A 29-year-old man has sudden severe chest pain, a heart rate of 132, and dilated pupils. Which history question is most important?
choices: Whether he has a family history of diabetes
Whether he has used cocaine or methamphetamine
Whether he has had a recent tetanus shot
Whether he exercises regularly
quiz.why: Stimulants cause coronary spasm and infarcts in people in their twenties and thirties, and patients rarely volunteer it unless asked plainly. The other questions do not change management for acute chest pain in this age group.

quiz.q: Which term describes a diabetic patient's infarct presenting as sudden dyspnea, sweating or vomiting with no chest pain?
choices: Prodromal angina
Referred pain
An anginal equivalent
Pleuritic presentation
quiz.why: An anginal equivalent is a symptom that substitutes for chest pain when neuropathy blunts the pain signal. Referred pain describes discomfort felt in a different location, not the absence of pain, and pleuritic refers specifically to pain that changes with breathing.

quiz.q: An ICD delivers an internal shock at approximately what energy, and how long after it recognizes the rhythm?
choices: 5-10 joules, immediately
360 joules, after 30 seconds
100-200 joules, within 1 second
25-40 joules, roughly 10-15 seconds after recognition
quiz.why: Internal shocks are far lower energy than external ones, about 25-40 joules, because the electrodes are already in the heart. The device takes roughly 10-15 seconds to confirm the rhythm and charge, which is why a patient may collapse briefly before it fires.

quiz.q: A patient with an ICD has received five shocks in the last two hours. This is called electrical storm and it may be caused by:
choices: A heart repeatedly entering a lethal rhythm, or the device firing at a non-lethal rhythm such as rapid atrial fibrillation
A depleted battery in every case
Normal device self-testing
Movement artifact from exercise
quiz.why: Three or more shocks in 24 hours is electrical storm, and it means either recurrent lethal rhythms or inappropriate shocks at a rhythm that is not lethal. Either one is an emergency requiring high-priority transport and ALS. Devices do not self-test by shocking the patient.

quiz.q: You feel a sharp tingle in your hands while compressing a patient whose ICD discharges. You should:
choices: Stop compressions until the device is deactivated with a magnet
Continue compressions; the sensation is startling but not dangerous
Remove your gloves and use a mechanical device only
Stop and check a pulse before resuming
quiz.why: The energy reaching your hands from an internal shock is small and harmless, even though it startles. Stopping compressions for it costs perfusion. Magnet use is a medical direction decision and is not a prerequisite for continuing CPR.

quiz.q: An LVAD patient is confused with new right-sided weakness. This should be treated as:
choices: A driveline infection
Expected behavior from low continuous flow
A stroke alert, since these patients are anticoagulated and have strokes from both clot and hemorrhage
A device alarm requiring a battery change
quiz.why: Anticoagulation means these patients suffer strokes in both directions, and sudden focal deficits are a stroke until proven otherwise. Confusion is not a normal state on a working device, and neither a battery nor a driveline infection produces sudden one-sided weakness.

quiz.q: Which resource should be contacted early on an LVAD call and is printed on the patient's equipment bag?
choices: The patient's primary care office
The nearest community hospital switchboard
The device manufacturer's sales line
The 24-hour VAD coordinator number
quiz.why: Every LVAD patient travels with a 24-hour VAD coordinator number, and calling it early is genuinely part of the care. The trained caregiver at the bedside is the other expert resource. A primary care office or a community hospital cannot troubleshoot the device.

quiz.q: Defibrillation of an LVAD patient with a shockable rhythm is:
choices: Performed normally with standard pad placement
Permitted only at reduced energy
Permitted only after the device is disconnected
Contraindicated because it damages the pump
quiz.why: Defibrillation is unrestricted in LVAD patients and uses standard placement. It is compressions that carry the historic caution, and even that is now narrowed to a stopped pump in an unresponsive, non-perfusing patient after troubleshooting fails.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old has a heart rate of 52 with mottled skin and delayed capillary refill despite an open airway, oxygen and effective ventilation. You should:
choices: Continue ventilating and reassess in five minutes
Begin chest compressions
Transport immediately without further intervention
Apply the AED and analyze
quiz.why: A rate under 60 with poor perfusion in a child, despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation, is treated like an arrest, and compressions begin before the pulse disappears. Waiting to reassess is how a preventable pediatric arrest becomes an actual one, and the AED is for a pulseless patient.

quiz.q: Which drowning patient requires spinal motion restriction?
choices: An adult who slipped on a pool deck but was never submerged
A swimmer who developed leg cramps in a lap pool
A teenager who dove headfirst into shallow water
A toddler found floating in a backyard pool with no witnessed fall
quiz.why: Restriction is based on mechanism, and a headfirst dive into shallow water is a classic cervical injury mechanism. Routine immobilization of every drowning victim delays resuscitation, which is what the question is testing.

quiz.q: Why is 15:2 used for two-rescuer pediatric CPR instead of 30:2?
choices: Children's hearts respond better to shorter compression cycles
It matches the adult ratio with an advanced airway
Children have smaller chests and tire the compressor faster
Pediatric arrest is usually hypoxic, so more frequent ventilation treats the underlying cause
quiz.why: The ratio exists because breathing is what failed in most pediatric arrests, so ventilation is the treatment, not a secondary task. Chest size and compressor fatigue do not drive the ratio, and the advanced airway pattern is continuous compressions with timed breaths.

quiz.q: At a core temperature near 28 C, why does prolonged downtime carry a better prognosis than it would in a warm patient?
choices: Cold slows metabolism so the brain needs far less oxygen
Cold prevents ventricular fibrillation
Cold stimulates the SA node to fire faster
Cold thins the blood, improving circulation
quiz.why: Reduced metabolic demand is the entire reason for the not dead until warm and dead rule. Cold actually makes the ventricle MORE irritable, not less, and it slows the heart rather than speeding it.

quiz.q: Where should heat packs be applied to a severely hypothermic patient, and why?
choices: Directly on the hands and feet, to restore circulation fastest
Wrapped and placed at the chest, neck, armpits and groin, to warm the trunk and avoid afterdrop
Directly on the skin of the back for maximum transfer
Nowhere; passive insulation only is always correct
quiz.why: Warming the limbs returns cold acidic blood to the core, dropping core temperature further, which is afterdrop. Trunk warming avoids that. Packs are always wrapped so they never touch skin directly, because a numb patient cannot feel a burn.

quiz.q: A hypothermic arrest patient receives one AED shock without conversion. You should:
choices: Transport without further analysis
Stop defibrillating until the core temperature exceeds 30 C
Continue CPR and follow the standard AED sequence while rewarming continues
Stop CPR since a cold heart will not respond
quiz.why: Current AHA guidance is to use the standard sequence while rewarming, rather than the older three-shock limit. A cold heart may not convert until warmer, and CPR continues regardless. Field termination rules generally do not apply to hypothermic arrest.

quiz.q: Which phrase is the correct way to inform a family of a death?
choices: We lost him
We were unable to obtain a pulse
He has passed on
He died
quiz.why: Plain words prevent genuine confusion; families hearing softened language sometimes ask whether their relative is still being treated. The recommended shape is a warning sentence, the fact using died or dead, then silence.

quiz.q: Which documentation is specifically important after a field termination?
choices: Downtime, rhythms, interventions, exact time of termination and who gave the order
The family's verbal consent to stop
The bystander's name only
Only the time of the call and the address
quiz.why: Downtime, rhythms, interventions, the exact termination time and the ordering physician are the record that matters, and equipment is left in place if the death may be investigated. Family consent is not the authority for termination.

quiz.q: An unwitnessed arrest received one AED shock and never regained a pulse. Which criterion of the BLS termination of resuscitation rule does this patient fail?
choices: That the arrest must not have been witnessed by EMS
That no shock may have been delivered by the AED
That there must be no ROSC after the defined period
That medical control contact is usually required
quiz.why: The rule needs all three: not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, and no ROSC. This arrest was unwitnessed and had no ROSC, so the only criterion that fails is the shock, because a shockable rhythm carries a better prognosis. Medical control contact is a separate policy requirement, not one of the three criteria.

quiz.q: Hospitals manage post-arrest patients with targeted temperature control in what range and for how long?
choices: Below 28 C until neurologic recovery
28-30 C for 6 hours
32-36 C for 24 hours
36-38 C for 48 hours
quiz.why: The standard is 32-36 C for 24 hours in the hospital. In the field your contribution is simply to avoid active warming and to prevent fever, since post-arrest fever is associated with worse neurologic outcomes. Do not pack a patient in ice unless protocol directs it.

quiz.q: A post-ROSC patient begins seizing and posturing during transport. This should be interpreted as:
choices: Evidence of a new stroke requiring immediate diversion
Proof of hypoglycemia
A sign that the resuscitation has failed and support should be withdrawn
A common post-arrest finding that is not a reason to stop supporting the patient
quiz.why: Seizure activity and posturing are common after global ischemia and do not predict the outcome on their own. They are not a reason to change destination or to stop supporting oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. Glucose is still worth checking, but it is not proven by posturing.

quiz.q: On the radio you should specifically say cardiac arrest with ROSC rather than chest pain because:
choices: It activates a different hospital team than a chest pain notification does
It is required by HIPAA
It determines the ambulance billing code
It shortens the report
quiz.why: The words determine which team is waiting, and post-arrest care is organized differently from a STEMI activation. Report length, privacy rules and billing have nothing to do with choosing those words.

quiz.q: A 72-year-old with chest pain has an SpO2 of 91% and mild shortness of breath. Oxygen therapy should be:
choices: Withheld, since routine oxygen is no longer given in chest pain
Given, because the saturation is below 94% and the patient is dyspneic
Given at 15 L/min regardless of the reading
Given only after nitroglycerin is administered
quiz.why: Oxygen in chest pain is indicated when the SpO2 is below 94%, when the patient is short of breath, or when they are in shock. This patient meets two of those. What was abandoned is routine oxygen for every chest pain patient, not oxygen for a hypoxic one.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old is wheezing with swollen ankles, distended neck veins, and crackles at both bases. Her only home medications are furosemide and lisinopril. The most likely cause of the wheezing is:
choices: Chronic bronchitis
A first asthma attack
Fluid from heart failure compressing the small airways
An allergic reaction to lisinopril
quiz.why: Wheezing in decompensated heart failure comes from fluid squeezing small airways, and the diuretic, the swelling, the neck veins and the crackles all point that way. A first asthma attack at 68 is rare, and lisinopril classically causes a dry cough rather than wheeze with volume overload.

quiz.q: During a resuscitation, when is the best moment to switch compressors?
choices: After every shock
Every 5 minutes to reduce total interruptions
Whenever the compressor reports feeling tired
During the rhythm analysis every 2 minutes, so no compression time is lost
quiz.why: Switching during the analysis costs no additional pause, and quality measurably falls before the compressor feels tired, which is why fatigue is a poor trigger. Every 5 minutes is too long, and switching after each shock would delay the immediate resumption of compressions.
